title: From Bending to Coiling: Mechanics and Thickness Evolution of Tentacle-Like Pneumatic Actuators
content: Soft tentacle-like actuators offer inherent compliance and versatility for safe interactions with humans and fragile objects. In this study, we investigate how material stiffness and air channel geometry affect coiling behavior in pneumatic soft actuators with embedded, off-axis channels. We designed actuators with varying stiffness by layering materials of different modulus and experimentally evaluated their bending and coiling responses under increasing internal pressure.Our results demonstrate a clear nonlinear inverse relationship between pressure and curvature: as pressure increases, curvature initially rises, peaks, and then drops due to loop formation. Stiffer layers enable higher peak curvatures and promote earlier onset of coiling at lower pressure levels, allowing actuators to wrap more tightly around smaller objects. Conversely, softer materials require significantly higher pressures to coil and exhibit limited curvature range.We identify two key operational regimes: high-curvature, low-pressure actuation for precise grasping with stiffer materials, and low-curvature, high-pressure operation for larger object manipulation using softer configurations. These findings reveal important trade-offs between material stiffness, curvature sensitivity, and actuation pressure, providing a design framework for optimizing soft robotic tentacles for targeted gripping tasks.Our results demonstrate a clear nonmonotonic relationship between pressure and curvature: curvature initially increases with pressure, reaches a maximum near loop closure, and subsequently decreases as the loop expands and self-contact redistributes the deformation.
